objectives: Summarize the key facts about Prophet Noah and their sources.
Explain how his people responded to his warning.
Explain the uncertainty about the 950 years.
Use in addition to + -ing, consequently and whether.
content.pedagogy: The opening chapter is dense with references: surahs, a report and a long Qur’anic quotation. A source map (claim → surah or report) shows how the writer supports each statement, and the final paragraph models careful, hedged writing (it is not clear whether …).
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter gives three possibilities for the 950 years; it does not choose one.
Noah warned his people about the punishment; the punishment was Allah’s decision, not his wish.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: in addition to + -ing · consequently · since (reason) · whether … or (noun clause)
Notice (Activity 1): In addition to accusing him of lying, they …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the words, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *In addition to accuse · *It is not clear if or not.
Use (Activity 4): patience in the face of adversity.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: u-LUL AZM, taw-HEED, tû-FAN, ri-vâ-YET, an-ka-BUT.
Stress: ex-TEN-sive-ly, re-BEL-lious, AD-ver-si-ty, LIFE-span.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can a writer show that a fact is certain or uncertain?”
duringReading: First reading: What are the key facts about Noah?
Second reading: complete the source map.
Find the three possibilities for the 950 years.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Source map; 18–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: patience in the face of adversity; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why does the writer give a surah for almost every claim?
What two demands did the people make?
Why is careful language important when the evidence is not clear?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ulul-Azm” and “A Grateful Servant” when the picture is in place.

Word Notes: extensively, determination, referred to, maintained, fall upon, rebellious, threaten, accusing, demanded, presence, grateful, in the face of adversity, provides, regarding, covers, lifespan, entire.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the source map with three claims written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short, hedged paragraph about the 950 years with whether and it is not clear.

formativeAssessment: Uses in addition to + -ing or whether correctly.
expectedResponses: Prophet Noah is one of the prophets of great determination. In addition to accusing him of lying, his people demanded that he remove his poor followers. It is not clear whether the 950 years covers his entire lifespan.
content.transferTask: Write about a person who showed patience in the face of adversity.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the three possibilities as the book gives them?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “in addition to + -ing” and one with “whether”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses in addition to or whether.

content.chapter: Chapter 2: The Flood in Ancient Accounts
objectives: Compare the Sumerian and Babylonian flood accounts.
Summarize the flood story in the Epic of Gilgamesh.
Explain what archaeological research suggests.
Use passive reporting and date back to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter presents ancient Middle Eastern flood accounts as historical texts. A comparison table (Sumerian tablet / Old Babylonian fragment / Epic of Gilgamesh) helps learners organize the details. Present these accounts as ancient texts, in the words of the book, without comparing them with the Qur’an.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Ziusudra and Uta-napishtim are the same figure in two languages, as the chapter explains.
In the epic, the gods wanted to destroy humankind because of noise; this is the epic’s view, not the book’s.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: passive reporting (was told that, was asked to) · date back to · participle clauses (consisting of) · research suggests that
Notice (Activity 1): King Ziusudra … was told that a flood was coming …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *dates back from · *consisted of just a few lines, was found · *research suggest.
Use (Activity 4): stories across cultures.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ZI-u-su-dra, u-ta-na-PISH-tim, GIL-ga-mesh, AK-kad, as-SYR-i-a, NI-sir, eu-PHRA-tes.
Stress: CU-ne-i-form, cat-AS-tro-phes, DEV-as-tat-ing, ex-CES-sive.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do historians learn about events from thousands of years ago?”
duringReading: First reading: Where are the oldest flood accounts found?
Second reading: complete the comparison table.
Find what archaeological research suggests.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Comparison table; 18–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: stories across cultures; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What do the Sumerian and Babylonian versions share?
Why is the Epic of Gilgamesh important for historians?
What does archaeology add to the written accounts?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Cuneiform” and “Ziusudra” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: date back to, Epic, immortality, excessive, devastating.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the comparison table with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short museum label for a cuneiform flood tablet.

expectedResponses: The earliest written records date back to the Sumerians. In the Sumerian version, Ziusudra was told that a flood was coming. Archaeological research suggests that Sumer and Akkad were affected by devastating floods.
content.transferTask: Write about a story that appears in different versions in different cultures.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners present the ancient accounts without comparing or judging?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “date back to” and one with “was told that”.

content.chapter: Chapter 3: The Flood in the Qur’an
objectives: Explain the two meanings of ‘Tûfan’ in the Qur’an.
Explain the debate about a global or local flood.
Explain the view the chapter presents and its reasoning.
Use whether-clauses, the view that and gerund subjects.
content.pedagogy: The chapter presents an argument: it gives the Qur’anic references, notes a debate, and reaches the view that the flood was regional. An argument map (evidence → reasoning → conclusion) helps learners follow the structure. Keep the discussion within the words of the book and do not add outside opinions.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The chapter says the Torah states the flood covered the entire world; it presents the regional view as generally accepted.
The reasoning is based on the verses that Noah was sent to his people.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: gerund phrase as subject · whether … or · the view that + clause · refer to · based on this
Notice (Activity 1): extending a catastrophe … is contrary to divine justice.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *Extending … are contrary · *the view which the flood was local.
Use (Activity 4): weighing different views.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: tû-FAN, fur-QAN, shu-’a-RA.
Stress: CON-tra-ry, do-MES-ti-cat-ed, di-VINE, re-GION-al.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do writers build an argument from evidence?”
duringReading: First reading: What does ‘Tûfan’ refer to?
Second reading: complete the argument map.
Find the view that is generally accepted.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Argument map; 18–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: weighing different views; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What evidence does the chapter give for a regional flood?
Why does the chapter mention divine justice?
What were the animals on the ark, according to the generally accepted view?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Tûfan” and “Wood and Nails” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: refers to, extending, contrary to, divine justice, domesticated.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the argument map with the conclusion written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a summary of the chapter’s argument in five sentences: evidence, reasoning and conclusion.

formativeAssessment: Explains the two meanings of Tûfan.
Uses whether or the view that correctly.
expectedResponses: Various views have been put forward regarding whether the flood was global or local. Based on the verses that Noah was sent to his people, the view that the flood was regional is generally accepted.
content.transferTask: Write about a question on which experts hold different views.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the discussion within the words of the book?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “whether” and one with “the view that”.

rubricLevels.secure: Uses whether or the view that.

content.chapter: Chapter 4: The Idols of Noah’s People
objectives: Explain how idolatry developed among Noah’s people.
Name the five idols.
Compare the chapter’s explanation with the hadith of Ibn Abbas.
Use not … until, the past perfect passive and turn … into.
content.pedagogy: The chapter explains the development of idolatry twice: once in the writer’s words and once through the hadith of Ibn Abbas. A comparison of the two explanations shows how the hadith adds detail (the places where they used to sit, Satan’s inspiration). Read the hadith and the verse as they are.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The statues were first made to remember righteous people; they were not idols at first.
The idols were used as mediators between people and Allah; people did not forget Allah completely.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: not … until · past perfect (active and passive) · turn A into B
Notice (Activity 1): The idols were not worshipped until those who made them died …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *were not worshipped since · *had been build · *turned them to objects.
Use (Activity 4): knowing the origin.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: ibn AB-bas, WAD, su-WA’, ya-GHUS, ya-’UK, NASR, bu-KHA-ri.
Stress: pros-PER-i-ty, ME-di-a-tors, ex-CEP-tion-al, PI-ous.
beforeReading: Ask: “How can a custom change its meaning over generations?”
duringReading: First reading: How did idolatry develop?
Second reading: compare the writer’s explanation and the hadith.
Find what the people believed the idols could do.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–18 Two explanations; 18–21 Quick Challenge; 21–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: knowing the origin; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: What did the people believe their gods could do?
What detail does the hadith add?
Why was forgetting the origin so important?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Ten Centuries” and “Mediators” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: companions, prosperity, abandon, Initially, righteous, displayed exceptional, deeds, mediators, idolatry, pious, inspired, origin.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a two-column chart: the writer / the hadith.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph that explains how idolatry developed, with not … until and the past perfect passive.

formativeAssessment: Uses not … until or the past perfect correctly.
expectedResponses: Initially, the names belonged to righteous individuals. After their deaths, statues were made of them. The idols were not worshipped until those who made them died and their origin was forgotten.
content.transferTask: Write about a custom whose origin many people have forgotten.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners see how forgetting the origin changed the meaning?

rubricLevels.secure: Uses not … until or the past perfect.

objectives: Explain Noah’s arguments from creation.
Explain why idol worship is unfair to the human mind, in Noah’s words.
Analyze how and why the elites responded.
Use would for past habits, so as not to and while for contrast.
content.pedagogy: The longest chapter combines arguments from nature (day and night, sun and moon), a critique of idol worship, the people’s reactions and two Qur’anic quotations. Divide it into four parts: arguments → reactions → elites → the verses. Learners analyze the elites’ motives with evidence; the verses are read as they are.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah’s arguments are based on reason and creation, not on force.
The elites first ignored the message; they felt threatened only when it spread among the poor.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: would + verb (past habits) · so as not to + verb · while (contrast) · respond by + -ing
Notice (Activity 1): Whenever Noah would come …, they would either run away or …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *so as to not hear · *responded with mocking · *While … but …
Use (Activity 4): thinking freely.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: lâ i-LÂ-he il-lal-LAH, SU-rah HÛD.
Stress: HAR-mo-ny, MEAS-ure-ment, FOS-ters, op-PRES-sion, CON-se-quen-ces.
beforeReading: Ask: “What can we learn about the world by observing day and night?”
duringReading: First reading: What arguments did Noah use?
Second reading: complete the four-part chart.
Find how the elites responded.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–13 First reading in four parts; 13–19 Four-part chart; 19–22 Quick Challenge; 22–36 Language Focus 1–3; 36–42 Use: thinking freely; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: How did Noah use nature to explain the Oneness of Allah?
Why does the chapter call idol worship “the enslavement of human beings”?
Why did the elites want things to stay the same?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Day and Night” and “Two Camps” when the picture is in place.

Word Notes: tirelessly, harmony, offers, measurement, fosters, leads, blind faith, enslavement, consequences, wrap, abandoned, exposed to, humiliation, oppression, opposing, responded by, worthless outsiders, plain, torment.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the four-part chart with the headings written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short analysis of the elites’ motives with three pieces of evidence from the chapter.

expectedResponses: Noah explained that the harmony of day and night shows Allah’s power. While the poor found comfort in his message, the elites rejected it. They would mock him, and they responded by attacking his followers.
content.transferTask: Write an argument about why free thinking is important today.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners support their analysis with evidence from the chapter?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “would” for a past habit and one with “so as not to”.

rubricLevels.notYet: Point to the first two paragraphs.

content.chapter: Chapter 6: The Wealthy Elite and the Poor Believers
objectives: Explain the elites’ condition.
Explain Noah’s answer and his reasons.
Explain what Noah’s way of thinking shows.
Use demand that + base verb and it is (not) someone’s right to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter shows a moral decision: the elites set a condition, and Noah refuses. The verses (Surah Hûd, 29–31) give Noah’s answer; read them as they are. The final paragraph interprets his answer as logical thinking without ego. A condition–response–reason chart helps learners analyze the scene.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah did not ask for any wealth; he said his reward is from Allah.
Noah did not claim to know the unseen or to be an angel.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: demand / insist that + base verb (subjunctive) · it is (not) someone’s right to + verb · appeal to
Notice (Activity 1): demanded that Noah abandon his poor … followers.
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *demanded that Noah abandons · *it was not his right driving them.
Use (Activity 4): standing by your principles.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: za-li-MEEN.
Stress: con-CES-sions, ap-PEALED, em-BRACE, be-STOW.
beforeReading: Ask: “Is it ever right to refuse a compromise?”
duringReading: First reading: What did the elites demand?
Second reading: complete the condition–response–reason chart.
Find what Noah’s way of thinking shows.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–11 First reading; 11–17 Chart; 17–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: standing by your principles; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the elites set this condition?
Why did Noah say it was not his right to drive the believers away?
What does “ignores one’s personal ego” mean?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Condition” and “Ego” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: appealed to, reason, embrace, reward, look down upon, bestow.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the chart with the condition written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a short analysis of why Noah’s answer is logical, using the last paragraph.

formativeAssessment: Explains the condition and the answer.
Uses demand that + base verb correctly.
expectedResponses: The wealthy elite demanded that Noah abandon his poor followers. Noah refused to make concessions, explaining that it was not his right to drive them away. This shows logical thinking that ignores one’s personal ego.
content.transferTask: Write about when we should refuse to make concessions.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners read the verses as they are?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “demanded that + base verb”.

content.chapter: Chapter 7: Nine Hundred and Fifty Years
objectives: Trace how the conflict grew.
Explain how Noah answered the insults.
Explain the events that led to Allah’s command to build the ark.
Use now that, after + clause and go on to.
content.pedagogy: The chapter alternates narration and verses. Learners follow the narration line (the conflict grows → 950 years → revelation → prayer → command) and read the verses as they are, without paraphrasing them. The calm answer of Noah is the key moment for discussion.
anticipatedMisconceptions: Noah prayed only after he received a revelation that no one else would believe.
Noah answered calmly; he did not insult the leaders back.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: now that + clause · after + clause · go on to + verb · grow + adjective
Notice (Activity 1): Now that the Prophet’s suffering had finally reached its limit, …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *now when · *went on calling (when the meaning is “next did”) · *grew more intensely.
Use (Activity 4): answering calmly.
content.pronunciationFocus:
Names: SU-rah HÛD, a’-RÂF, NÛH.
Stress: re-VE-la-tion, GRIEV-ing, a-STRAY, IN-ten-si-ty.
beforeReading: Ask: “How do you usually react when someone insults you?”
duringReading: First reading: How did the conflict grow?
Second reading: follow the narration line between the verses.
Find how Noah answered.
content.lessonPlan: 0–5 Hook; 5–12 First reading; 12–17 Narration line; 17–20 Quick Challenge; 20–35 Language Focus 1–3; 35–42 Use: answering calmly; 42–45 Exit ticket.
discussionPoints: Why did the unbelievers start acting rudely?
What does “as prophets do” tell us about prophets?
Why did Noah pray only at the end?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “Calm Answers” and “The Limit” when the picture is in place.
Word Notes: benefit, astray, grieving.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give the narration line with the first step written in.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Write a paragraph that traces the conflict in five steps, using after and now that.

formativeAssessment: Uses now that or after correctly.
expectedResponses: After all of their arguments failed, the unbelievers started acting rudely. Noah answered calmly and went on to call his people for 950 years. Now that his suffering had reached its limit, he turned to Allah in prayer.
content.transferTask: Write about why answering insults calmly is wise.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners follow the narration without paraphrasing the verses?

objectives: Describe how Noah built the ark.
Explain how and why the people mocked him.
Explain Noah’s answer in the verse.
Use be supposed to, keep + -ing and after + -ing.
content.pedagogy: A short, vivid chapter. The people’s rhetorical questions show mockery; the verse (Surah Hûd, 38–39) gives Noah’s answer. Learners analyze the questions as mockery, not as real questions. Never act out the prophet; learners analyze the language only.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The people’s questions were mockery, not real questions.
Noah built the ark by Allah’s command, far from the sea.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: be supposed to · keep + -ing · after + -ing · give up + -ing · rhetorical questions
Notice (Activity 1): … or is the wind supposed to move it for you?
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.
Likely errors: *kept to make fun · *give up to be · *After gather.
Use (Activity 4): mockery and persistence.

Find Noah’s answer in the verse.

What did Noah say they would know?
interactiveTips: Use the picture hotspots “A Remote Location” and “Mockery” when the picture is in place.

differentiation.strugglingLearners: Give a chart: question / what it really means.
differentiation.fastFinishers: Rewrite each mocking question as a statement that shows what the people really meant.

formativeAssessment: Describes how Noah built the ark.
Uses keep + -ing or be supposed to correctly.
expectedResponses: After gathering wood and tools, Noah worked tirelessly to construct the ark. The people kept making fun of him and asked if the wind was supposed to move it. Their questions were mockery.
content.transferTask: Write about how mockery affects people and how they can respond.
content.teacherReflection: Did learners analyze the questions as mockery?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “be supposed to”.

rubricLevels.secure: Describes the building of the ark.
Uses keep + -ing or be supposed to.

objectives: Describe how the flood began.
Explain the sign in the report.
Explain the crowd’s reaction.
Use must have + past participle and participle clauses.

Use (Activity 4): wrong conclusions.

content.teacherReflection: Did learners keep the words “according to a report”?

exitTicket: Write one sentence with “must have + past participle”.

objectives: Explain who refused to join Noah on the ark.
Report the different scholarly views accurately.
Explain why the writer does not choose one view.
Use reporting verbs and while for contrast.
content.pedagogy: A short chapter that models fair academic reporting: three sources, three numbers, three reporting verbs. Learners practice reporting views without choosing one.
anticipatedMisconceptions: The writer does not say which number is correct.
Being Noah’s wife or son did not change their choice; they rejected the faith themselves.
content.grammarFocus:
Targets: reporting verbs (note, mention, suggest) · while (contrast) · hold a view · choose (not) to
Notice (Activity 1): While Ibn Abbas noted …, some mentioned … other accounts suggest …
Build (Activities 2–3): choose the forms, then rewrite.

Use (Activity 4): reporting views fairly.

Use (Activity 4): the power of nature.

content.chapter: Chapter 12: The Believers Come Ashore and Ashura
objectives: Describe what the believers did after they left the ark.
Explain why the fire was a relief.

metadata.title: Noah B2 — Teacher’s Book
metadata.subtitle: Prophet Noah (pbuh)
metadata.estimatedDuration: 13 chapter units of 45 minutes each. Whole-book review pages follow separately.
metadata.targetLearners: Learners who can follow extended texts about history, ideas and values, and who can produce clear, detailed explanations, evaluations and arguments.
metadata.purpose: Develop evidence-based B2 reading, listening, speaking and writing through the story of Prophet Noah: his place in the Qur’an, the ancient flood accounts, the Qur’anic view of the flood, the origin of idolatry, his call and the conflict with the elite, the ark, the flood, Ashura and his last advice, using the Language Focus attached to every story chapter.
metadata.approachDesc: Every story chapter follows the TYMM route. YDAB1 listening and YDAB2 reading establish meaning and evidence; the Quick Challenge checks comprehension. Grammar is then learned inductively: in the Language Focus, learners first NOTICE a form in a real chapter sentence and work out what it does, then BUILD it in controlled, meaningful practice, and finally USE it in connected YDAB3 speaking and YDAB4 writing about their own world. At B2, learners also notice how the writer signals certainty (according to a report / suggests / it is not clear whether / the view that … is generally accepted) and builds an argument, and they use these forms in their own writing.
metadata.assessmentEvidence: 13 Quick Challenges, text-evidence checks, chapter Language Focus tasks (Notice → Build → Use), exit tickets, Knowledge Check, Vocabulary Challenge, Language Review and Final Challenge.

formative: Short spoken and written Use tasks

readingFramework.before: Activate only what the chapter needs: a short question, a map, a date or a picture of the sea.
readingFramework.during: Listen first for gist (when the audio is ready), then read and follow the chapter’s own structure: a source map, a comparison of ancient accounts, an argument, two explanations, narration between verses, a timeline or a hadith with its sources.
readingFramework.after: Complete the Quick Challenge, then the chapter’s Language Focus (notice → build → use), then a connected B2 transfer: an explanation, evaluation or argument about the learners’ own world.

vocabularyApproach.selection: Word Notes are the bold words of the teacher-approved text. Prioritize them and the words needed for the chapter’s key idea.
vocabularyApproach.method: Infer meaning from context or a picture before any direct explanation.
vocabularyApproach.recycling: Reuse vocabulary in Language Focus tasks, exit tickets and the Language Review.

metadata.grammarApproach: Inductive and text-based. Start from the story sentence, ask a meaning question (What does this form tell us? How certain is the writer?), let learners formulate the rule, then confirm it and practice it in context. B2 targets include the subjunctive after demand, modals of deduction, participle and result clauses, the past perfect continuous, gerund subjects, whether-clauses and formal linkers. Rule explanations appear in the app only after learners answer.
grammarSequence: Ch1: in addition to + -ing · consequently · since (reason) · whether … or (noun clause)
Ch2: passive reporting (was told that, was asked to) · date back to · participle clauses (consisting of) · research suggests that
Ch3: gerund phrase as subject · whether … or · the view that + clause · refer to · based on this
Ch4: not … until · past perfect (active and passive) · turn A into B
Ch5: would + verb (past habits) · so as not to + verb · while (contrast) · respond by + -ing
Ch6: demand / insist that + base verb (subjunctive) · it is (not) someone’s right to + verb · appeal to
Ch7: now that + clause · after + clause · go on to + verb · grow + adjective
Ch8: be supposed to · keep + -ing · after + -ing · give up + -ing · rhetorical questions
Ch9: must have + past participle (deduction) · present participle clauses · once (= as soon as)
Ch10: reporting verbs (note, mention, suggest) · while (contrast) · hold a view · choose (not) to
Ch11: -ing result clauses (causing, flooding) · not a single · once again
Ch12: prevent … from + -ing · used to + verb · past perfect continuous (had been fasting since) · be made + adjective
Ch13: warn against + -ing · advise someone to + verb · the former / the latter · -ing result clauses (leaving us …)

valuesFocus: D12 Patience — Patience in the face of adversity.

languageFocus: Every one of the 13 chapters has a Language Focus set built as Notice → Build → Use (4 activities).
Use the Language Focus after basic comprehension and the Quick Challenge.
Always start from the story sentence and ask a meaning question before naming the form.
The Use step is connected spoken or written production about a new, non-story situation.
metadata.differentiationNotes: Reduce linguistic load without lowering the reasoning target: one paragraph at a time, charts given in part, selected vocabulary, audio replay, sentence frames and oral rehearsal. Extend by asking for evaluation, counterpoints and evidence from more than one chapter, not by introducing outside facts.

sensitiveNotes.title: Source fidelity and respectful teaching
notes: Keep explanations within the wording of the book; do not add outside details or opinions.
Never draw or act out Prophet Noah or any prophet. Posters and panels use words, quotations, the ark, the water, the land and the animals only.
The Qur’an quotations, the hadiths and their sources belong to the teacher-approved text; they are read as they are, without extra comment, and the exercises do not change their words.
Chapter 2 presents ancient Sumerian and Babylonian accounts; present them in the words of the book, without comparing or judging.
Chapter 3 presents the debate about a global or local flood and the view that is generally accepted; keep the discussion within the words of the book.
Chapters 9, 10 and 12 use “according to a report”, “suggest” and different numbers; present these as the book gives them.
Read the parts about the punishment and about Noah’s son calmly, in the words of the book.

metadata.title: Noah B2 — Self-Study Guide
metadata.subtitle: Read • Find • Check • Build • Use
metadata.estimatedStudyTime: About 30 minutes per chapter, plus the review pages at the end
metadata.whoIsThisFor: B2 learners who study the story of Prophet Noah alone or with a teacher.
learningGoals: Find evidence in the text before answering.
Follow the story of Prophet Noah and its sources in extended texts.
Evaluate the lessons of patience, justice and humility with evidence from the book.
Use each chapter’s Language Focus in connected sentences.
recommendedUse: Study one chapter at a time.
Read (and listen, when the audio is ready) before the Quick Challenge.
Repair wrong answers with the text.
Do the Language Focus after you understand the chapter.
Do the review pages after Chapter 13.

readingDiary.intro: Keep this diary when you finish the book. Write short answers.
prompts: The date I finished the book:
My favorite chapter, and one reason:
One lesson from the story of Prophet Noah that I think is still relevant today, and why:
One sentence for a friend: “Read this book because …”
One new word I want to keep:
The next book I want to read in the library:

sections.title: 1. Make Your Plan
sections.text: This book has 13 chapters. Plan the whole book before Chapter 1.
points: Choose your study days and how many chapters you will read each week.
Write one personal goal for this book.
Save new words to My words and review them after one day, three days and one week.

sections.title: 2. One Chapter per Session
sections.text: Each chapter takes about 30 minutes. Open “Study Path” for the steps of your chapter.
points: Preview the title and the “Before You Read” question.
Read for the main idea.
Find the evidence.
Do the Quick Challenge.
Do the Language Focus.

sections.title: 3. Read and Listen
sections.text: Read every chapter twice: once for the main idea, once for the details. When the audio is ready, listen once while you follow the text.
points: First reading: What is the chapter about?
Second reading: Mark names, dates and linking words.
Say one long sentence aloud with the right pauses.

sections.title: 4. Word Notes
sections.text: Bold words have Word Notes. Use them after you have tried to understand the sentence yourself.
points: Guess the meaning from the sentence.
Check the Word Note.
Write the word in a new sentence of your own.

sections.title: 5. Quick Challenge
sections.text: Answer before you read the feedback. If you are wrong, repair the answer with the text.
points: Find the paragraph the question is about.
Read the key sentence again.
Explain why the right answer is right, then try again.

sections.title: 6. Language Focus
sections.text: Each chapter has 4 Language Focus activities built from the chapter’s own sentences.
points: Activity 1 (Notice): Look at a sentence and what it means.
Activities 2–3 (Build): Choose, complete, correct or rewrite forms.
Activity 4 (Use): Write or say connected sentences about a different situation.

sections.title: 7. When It Is Hard
sections.text: Some chapters have many names and dates. Change how you study, not your goal.
points: Read one paragraph only.
Make a time line of the dates.
List the names and what each one did.
Learn only three words today.

sections.title: 8. Values in the Book
sections.text: The book shows patience, justice, humility and diligence. Find the sentence first, then think of a small action of your own.
points: Patience: Patience: Noah’s patience in the face of adversity has been given as an example, and as soon as he recovered, he returned to his mission (Chapters 1 and 5).
Justice: Justice: Noah refused to make concessions and said it was not his right to drive the believers away (Chapter 6).
Humility: Humility: Noah’s answer ignores personal ego, and he warned his sons against pride (Chapters 6 and 13).
Diligence: Diligence: Noah worked tirelessly day and night to construct the ark (Chapter 8).

sections.title: 9. At the End of the Book
sections.text: After Chapter 13, do the review pages in this order. Go back to a chapter when an answer is not clear.
points: Knowledge Check
Vocabulary Challenge
Master Glossary
Language Review
Final Challenge

sections.title: 10. Look Back
sections.text: Before Chapter 1 and again at the end, answer the “I can” statements of a few chapters. What can you do now that you could not do before?
points: Which chapter changed what you knew?
Explain to someone at home in six sentences the story of Noah and why its lessons still matter, in your home language or in English.
